progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | A A | Dm Dm |
metaLine: 84 BPM · 4/4 · one of the slower zemirot, sung sitting, usually late in the meal · five stanzas, each answered by the two-line refrain
intro: The one zemer at the Friday night table that is not in Hebrew. Israel Najara wrote it in Aramaic in sixteenth-century Safed, and its first letters spell his name. Aramaic is close enough to Hebrew that a learner can follow most of it and far enough that the differences jump out: the definite article is a final vowel instead of a prefix, the relative particle is a single syllable, and the word for "you" is not the one you have been taught. Singing it once teaches you more about the relation between the two languages than a chapter would.

stanzas.label: refrain

lines.en: God, Master of this world and all worlds,
You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: Four features of Aramaic in nine words. {{0.3}} ends in the vowel that means "the" — the article is a suffix, not a prefix. {{1.0}} is "you", where Hebrew says atah. {{1.2}} and {{1.4}} are king and kings with the same final vowel doing the same work. Learn this refrain and the rest of the poem stops being foreign.

stanzas.label: the work of Your might

lines.en: The work of Your might and Your wonders —
it is fitting to declare it before You.
God, Master of this world and all worlds, You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: {{3.1}} means "before You", and the root is the same one behind kodem, "earlier" — a word that means both in front of in space and before in time. The stanza is two lines long, which is the shortest in the poem.

stanzas.label: morning and evening

lines.en: Praises I will set in order, morning and evening,
to You, holy God, who created every living soul:
holy angels and human beings,
the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven.
God, Master of this world and all worlds, You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: {{8.0}} through {{8.3}} is the same list Genesis 1 makes, in the same order, and {{7.0}} is a word from Daniel — the only book of the Tanakh with substantial Aramaic in it, which is where Najara got the register.

stanzas.label: great are Your works

lines.en: Great are Your works and mighty,
bringing down the haughty and raising up the bent;
were a man to live a thousand years,
he could not enter Your might into any reckoning.
God, Master of this world and all worlds, You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: {{11.0}} and {{11.2}} are opposites in the same line — bringing down, lifting up — which is the shape of Hannah's song and of Psalm 146, both in Hebrew. Najara is translating a Hebrew habit into Aramaic and it survives the crossing intact.

stanzas.label: rescue Your flock

lines.en: God, to whom belong honour and greatness,
rescue Your flock from the mouth of the lions,
and bring Your people out from within exile,
Your people whom You chose out of all the nations.
God, Master of this world and all worlds, You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: The lions are Daniel's, and the exile named in {{17.4}} is the one Najara was living in — he wrote this in Safed, in an Ottoman province, four hundred years after the poem's Hebrew cousins. {{16.1}} and {{17.1}} are the Aramaic object marker, the equivalent of Hebrew et, and this is the clearest place in the poem to see the two languages side by side.

stanzas.label: to Your sanctuary

lines.en: To Your sanctuary return, and to the Holy of Holies,
the place where spirits and souls will rejoice,
and they will sing to You songs and whispers,
in Jerusalem, city of beauty.
God, Master of this world and all worlds, You are the King, King of kings.

stanzas.summary: {{22.2}} is songs and {{22.3}} is whispers, and pairing them is the poem's last move: the loud and the almost inaudible, both counted as singing. Then one place name and it stops.

chantTips: Slower than the other zemirot, and it stays slow. Around 84 BPM, sung sitting, usually after the faster ones have run their course.
The refrain is nine words and returns five times. Everyone sings it; the stanzas belong to whoever knows them.
The Aramaic will trip a Hebrew reader on the vowels rather than the letters. If you are learning it, learn the refrain by ear before you try to read it.
Many Sephardi and Mizrahi communities sing it to a maqam-based melody rather than the Ashkenazi one, and the two sound nothing alike. Both are correct.

about.body: The first letters of the five stanzas after the refrain spell the poet's name, Israel. He signed his poems this way as a matter of course, which is how the authorship of a sixteenth-century table song is known at all.

Najara worked in Safed among kabbalists for whom Aramaic was the language of the Zohar, and writing a table song in it placed the Friday night meal in that register. It is also the language of the Kaddish, so the sound was familiar to everyone at the table even if the grammar was not.

about.h: A poem with no Sabbath in it
about.body: Nothing in Yah Ribon mentions the Sabbath. It is sung on Friday night by custom rather than by subject, which sets it apart from every other zemer on this site — those are about the day; this one is about the world.
